text:
I need to tell our staff that we're ending fully remote work. I'm one of the three partners at an architecture firm with 46 architects and designers.

What I can say:
- From September 1, everyone works in the office on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
- 15 of our people were hired as fully remote in 2021 and 2022. 4 of them live more than two hours from the office.
- Those 4 can keep working remotely until the end of next year. After that, they come in once a week.
- Last year we lost two large hospital projects in the final interview. Both clients told us our team seemed not to know each other.
- Based on our review records, junior staff hired since 2022 are taking about 30% longer to reach the point where they lead a project.
- The partners have been coming in one day a week. We'll be in all three days too.

Keep it to one page. It goes out by email before an all-staff meeting on Friday.

Before I draft, a few questions. The answers will change what the email says, especially to the 15 people hired as remote.

1. **The other 11 remote hires.** They were hired as fully remote but live within two hours, so from September they come in three days a week. What do their contracts say about where they work? Are you offering them anything, like help with travel costs, a longer lead-in, or a way to ask for an exception? If someone decides they can't do it, what happens? They're the readers most likely to feel the deal has been broken, so the email needs a direct answer for them.

2. **Exceptions and flexibility for everyone else.** Can people pick their own hours on office days? Is there a way to ask for an exception for caregiving, health or disability? Do Monday and Friday stay fully remote?

3. **What the three office days will be used for.** Will the partners commit to anything specific, such as design reviews, pin-ups, mentoring juniors, or bringing project teams together? People will ask "why come in just to sit on video calls?" A concrete answer is the best reply.

4. **Dates and review.** Today is November 2026, so I'm reading this as **September 1, 2027**, with the 4 long-distance staff remote until **December 31, 2027** and then in once a week. Is that right? Will you commit to reviewing the policy at a set date? If so, how will you judge whether it's working?

5. **Sign-off and the meeting.** Who signs: you alone, or all three partners by name? What time is Friday's meeting, and will remote staff be able to join by video?

6. **What staff already know or will find out.** Is there anything that would weaken the case if it came out later? For example: does the office have desks for all 46 people? Did other things contribute to losing the hospital bids? Have there been recent pay freezes or departures? Is the 30% figure based on a small number of people?

If you don't know some of these, just say so and I'll write without them.

1. I don't know what their contracts say. We'll pay up to $150 a month toward commuting for anyone who lives more than 30 miles away. No exceptions beyond the 4 long-distance people. I don't know what happens if someone can't do it.

2. I don't know about hours or Mondays and Fridays. No exceptions beyond those 4.

3. I don't know. Nothing specific has been committed.

4. Yes, September 1, 2027, and the 4 stay remote until December 31, 2027. We'll review the policy with staff after six months. I don't know how we'd judge it.

5. Just me, Paul Whitaker. The meeting is Friday at 10 a.m. in the main studio. I don't know about video. Questions before the meeting can come to me or HR.

6. We don't have a desk for everyone yet. New desks arrive in August. I don't know about the other points.

<final_document>
Subject: Returning to the office three days a week from September 1, 2027

To everyone,

Starting September 1, 2027, everyone at the firm will work in the office on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. That includes all three partners. We'll talk it through together at Friday's meeting, but I wanted you to have the details in writing first.

**Why we're doing this**

Two things in our own records persuaded us.

Last year we lost two large hospital projects in the final interview. Both clients gave us the same reason: our team seemed not to know each other. These were projects we had worked hard for and could have won, and we lost them on how we came across as a team.

Our review records also show that junior staff hired since 2022 are taking about 30% longer to reach the point where they lead a project. That's not on them. Much of how architects learn happens by sitting near more experienced people: overhearing a call with a client, getting quick feedback over a drawing, watching how a problem gets solved. We haven't been giving our newer people enough of that.

The partners haven't set a good example either. We've been coming in one day a week. That changes too: from September, all three of us will be in on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.

**To the 15 of you hired as fully remote**

You joined us in 2021 and 2022 on the understanding that you would work remotely, and this changes that. I know that's a real cost, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Four of you live more than two hours from the office. You can keep working fully remotely until December 31, 2027. From January 2028 you'll come in one day a week.

For the rest of you, the three-day schedule applies from September 1. If this creates a serious problem for you, please talk to me or HR directly and soon. I would rather hear it now than in August.

**Support with commuting**

The firm will pay up to $150 a month toward commuting costs for anyone who lives more than 30 miles from the office.

**Desks**

Right now we don't have a desk for everyone. New desks arrive in August, before the policy starts.

**Exceptions and review**

Apart from the four long-distance colleagues above, there are no exceptions to the three-day schedule. Six months after it starts, we'll review the policy with you and listen to what is and isn't working.

**Friday**

We'll meet at 10 a.m. on Friday in the main studio. Please bring your questions. If you'd like to raise something before then, or privately, you can come to me or to HR.

Paul Whitaker
Partner
</final_document>

A few things to check before you send it:

- **The meeting date.** I left it as "Friday." If you'd like the date in the email, add it.
- **Gaps people will ask about on Friday.** You didn't know four things, so the email doesn't cover them. Expect questions on all four:
  - what happens if one of the 11 nearby remote hires can't make the schedule work
  - whether hours are flexible on office days, and what happens on Mondays and Fridays
  - what the three office days will actually be used for
  - how the six-month review will judge whether the policy is working
- **The strongest answer you could add.** The partners committing to something specific on office days, such as weekly design reviews or mentoring time with juniors, would do the most to answer "why come in?"
- **Contracts.** Have HR or a lawyer read the remote hires' contracts before this goes out. If any of them guarantee remote work, the email and the September date may need to change.
- **Video for Friday.** If remote staff can join the meeting by video, say so in the email. If they can't, they'll notice.
